Published 7:22 am Monday, November 3, 2025
Savannah rides a tariff-fueled surge while Brunswick’s auto trade hits the brakes. The Georgia Ports Authority is doing what it does best: moving cargo, even as President Donald Trump’s second term tariff storm rolls across the global trade horizon. The Port of Savannah’s container docks are humming, while Brunswick’s auto terminals are taking a hit. It’s a tale of two ports, one booming, one bracing.
The numbers tell the story. Savannah moved 5.7 million containers in fiscal 2025, up 8.6% from the year before — the second-busiest year in port history. Since 2016, its traffic has grown at a 4.5% annual clip, outpacing the national port average of 2.7%.
September alone saw 486,000 boxes, up 8% year over year. rail lifts jumped 21%, and trucks rolled through 316,000 gate transactions with a brisk 50-minute turnaround.
So much for tariffs killing trade. In Savannah, the opposite is happening.
The surge, ironically, is a side effect of the tariff threat itself. Importers, worried about cost hikes, rushed to get goods into the country before the new duties kicked in. The Atlanta Journal- Constitution reported that Savannah’s traffic “returned at near-record volumes” after a brief slowdown tied to Mr. Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs. The Associated Press added that retailers “scrambled to stock up,” creating an artificial wave of imports.
Nationwide, ports saw double-digit import jumps in early 2025. Savannah was one of the big winners. But these front-loaded shipments can’t last forever. GPA officials expect the pace to ease later this year once warehouses are full and the panic buying subsides.

The Georgia Chamber has pledged to continue supporting state businesses through what it calls a "quickly evolving global trade landscape." In February, the chamber launched its Global Business Subcommittee to offer coordination and advocacy.

Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America (HMGMA) is an electric vehicle (EV) production site operated by Hyundai and located in Ellabell, Bryan County, Georgia, United States. The $7.6 billion campus was built along Interstate 16 about 25 miles (40 km) west of downtown Savannah, with over 16 million square feet (1.5 million m2) of factory floor space. The company will also produce batteries in a joint venture with LG Energy Solution at a separate site now under construction.
The land occupied by HMGMA was previously designated by Bryan County as the Bryan County Mega Site. Volvo had considered the area for a new manufacturing plant in 2015, but ultimately built a factory in South Carolina instead.[2] Six years later, with hopes of successfully attracting a large manufacturer or an automaker, the area was purchased in 2021 for $61 million by the state of Georgia, Bryan and Chatham counties, and the Savannah Harbor-Interstate 16 Corridor Joint Development Authority;[a] the deal combined three separately-owned parcels of land. The site lies directly off of Interstate 16, with existing Class I rail links and close access to Interstate 95 and the Port of Savannah.[4]

“The Port of Brunswick is more than just a commercial hub – it’s essential to the livelihood of local families. When we see those ships coming in, they’re not just cars, but they represent jobs,” he said. “The port is the bloodline to the Brunswick community.”
Johnson explained that while the full impact of the tariffs remains uncertain, there are concerns from longshoremen about how their work may change. Many local workers depend on the port for their jobs, and tariffs could significantly affect their livelihoods.
“Longshoremen will obviously see their business model change,” Johnson said. “We’re producing products that have to find customers, and those customers, nine times out of 10, are outside our nation. We’re working with companies worldwide to ensure the port remains efficient and allows for expansion.”
